claims.text: Chainguard secures from the bottom up: rebuilt from source, minimal images, a managed process, and it stops where the application starts.
claims.quote: Rebuilt from source, minimal images, a managed process, and it stops where the application starts.

claims.text: Bottom up has three gaps: code the application never runs, assurance that depends on testing, and the loop of granting more when something breaks.
claims.quote: But bottom up has three gaps, and the conversation today made them clearer.

claims.text: In most images the code the application never runs is the large majority, and every one of those files is attack surface.
claims.quote: My estimate is that in most images it is the large majority

claims.text: The one case measured found about 70% of the files in the dependency tree never ran.
claims.quote: found about 70% of the files in the dependency tree never ran

value.unit: percent of files that never ran

claims.text: Chainguard's Custom Assembly only allows adding packages to an image; its documentation says packages in the source image cannot be removed by default.
claims.quote: only allows you to add packages into a given container image

claims.text: Come from the other end and ask one question at every layer: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs; keep that and remove everything else.
claims.quote: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs?

claims.text: The immutable line is the level below which nothing changes; the higher it is drawn, the more of the system is fixed, exact and small.
claims.quote: The higher you can draw the line below which nothing changes, the immutable line, the more of the system is fixed, exact and small.

claims.text: The method has the same shape as the code review model: a node the code has and no story asked for is a question for the author in a review, and code to remove in an image.
claims.quote: In a code review that is a question for the author. In an image, it is code to remove.

claims.text: Keeping only the code the use case runs kills living off the land, because an attacker inside a process has very little left to use.
claims.quote: If the only code on the box is the code the use case runs, there is very little to live off.

claims.text: For sgit 0.21.0 and its four dependencies, one CI-style use case under coverage cut the tree from 1,500 files to 428.
claims.quote: The tree was much smaller. 1,500 files became 428.

claims.text: Of 1,416 Python files, 418 had run, and the Python source went from 4.72 MB to 1.98 MB.
claims.quote: Of 1,416 Python files, 418 had run, and the Python source went from 4.72 MB to 1.98 MB.

claims.text: The use case passed from the minimal tree: the manifest came back from the scoped clone and the decrypted file read secret.
claims.quote: The use case passed from the minimal tree

claims.text: Commands outside the use case, sgit history log and sgit vault backup, failed with ModuleNotFoundError because the code they needed had been removed.
claims.quote: because the code they needed had been removed

claims.text: Years ago the same method by hand shrank Python deployments for Lambda functions by, as remembered, close to 90% of the dependency code.
claims.quote: the cut, as I remember it, was close to 90% of the dependency code

value.unit: percent of dependency code removed, from memory

claims.text: 14.78 MB of the dependencies is compiled, three quarters of the whole, almost all of it the 14.4 MB Rust binary inside cryptography, which coverage cannot see inside.
claims.quote: almost all of it is one file: the 14.4 MB Rust binary inside cryptography

claims.text: Coverage was not enough: cffi ran no Python code but removing its compiled backend broke the use case, and the tests caught what the coverage missed.
claims.quote: The tests caught what the coverage missed, which is the point of the method.

claims.text: Inside the 418 files that ran, only 38% of the statements executed, so files are a coarse unit of removal.
claims.quote: only 38% of the statements executed

value.unit: percent of statements executed in kept files

claims.text: Function-level removal would cut much more than file-level, and that is where a semantic graph of the code, function by function, earns its place.
claims.quote: Function-level removal would cut much more than file-level

claims.text: What changed is that understanding what each layer is for is now the part models are good at, and the result can be held as a fractal semantic graph from story to operating system.
claims.quote: is now the part models are good at

claims.text: The build is deterministic where it matters: the graph says what to keep, the build keeps exactly that, and the tests prove the use case still works.
claims.quote: The graph says what should be kept; the build keeps exactly that; the tests prove the use case still works.

claims.text: Minimising containers is a real field already: SlimToolkit and RapidFort watch what a container touches at run time and build a smaller image.
claims.quote: minimising containers is a real field already

claims.text: SlimToolkit, formerly DockerSlim and now a CNCF Sandbox project, builds a smaller image by up to 30 times in its own words.
claims.quote: by up to 30 times in its own words

value.unit: times smaller, by SlimToolkit's own figure

claims.text: The proposal starts from what the application is for rather than from what a container did; runtime observation is one input to it, not the whole of it.
claims.quote: Runtime observation is one input to that, not the whole of it.

claims.text: In a build that keeps only the code a use case needs, a vulnerability in removed code is a line in the record saying the code is absent, which a third party can certify.
claims.quote: it is a line in the record saying the code is absent

claims.text: Chainguard is unusually well placed to offer the certified top-down build and should build it or partner with whoever does, since built on top of their platform it could eventually deploy without the base images.
claims.quote: which is why I think they should build it, or partner with whoever does

claims.text: One tool, one use case: sgit and four dependencies, measured once; the Python runtime and the operating system were not measured.
claims.quote: sgit and four dependencies, measured once

claims.text: The 70% to 90% figures are estimates and memory: the Lambda result is from memory and the 70% is this measurement's share of files that never ran.
claims.quote: My Lambda result is from memory

claims.text: Chainguard's plans are not public to the author; that they do not do this comes from their public pages and one conversation, and they may be working on it.
claims.quote: they may be working on it

claims.text: SlimToolkit's and RapidFort's figures are their own and were not tested here.
claims.quote: I have not tested them here.

claims.text: A use case is only as complete as its tests: anything the tests do not exercise is removed, so the test suite becomes the definition of the application.
claims.quote: the test suite becomes the definition of the application

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo on 14 October 2026 after a conversation at Chainguard's event, and the measurement was run for it under coverage 7 across the whole dependency tree.
claims.quote: A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, after a conversation at Chainguard's event
